To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
small species that are long‐lived experience larger costs of immune activation.

(1) animals do incur costs of immune activity; (2) small, long‐lived animals pay the highest costs; and (3) the costs of immune activation are not as strongly influenced by body mass as by life‐history orientation.
Immune costs are appreciable, and small species and long‐lived animals pay higher immune activation cost than large and short‐lived ones, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the costs of immune activation in animals and how these costs vary across species.
the costs of immune activation.
the costs and benefits of immunity in animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
immune costs are a function of body size and life history, and this is likely to be the case for all animals, not just the ones studied here.
the costs of immunity have influenced the evolution, and that these costs are related to host life history.
immune activation costs are real and that they are related to host life history and size.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the costs of mounting immune responses are related, in part, to the life histories of animals, such that long‐ and small‐lived species incur larger costs of immune activation than short‐ and large‐lived species.
immune costs do matter, but that the magnitude of these costs varies across species.
immune costs are real, and that they are influenced by body size and longevity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
costs of immune responses are not trivial and that they can be substantial, particularly for small species that live long and are exposed to many parasites.
the costs of mounting an immune response can be appreciable, and that the costs of defense are not distributed evenly among animals.
costs of immune activation are substantial, and that these costs can be substantial even in the face of high parasite burdens and high fitness costs of infection.
